evidence.fact: Listed as trad/alpine, 24 pitches, Grade V; with a 70 m rope the bypass ledges take 2 pitches and the route 24.

facts.value: V

evidence.fact: Route listed as Grade V.
Route rated V, 5.9-10a, 2500 feet.
Page title gives the route as 2500 feet long.

facts.value: Fred Beckey et al., 1963

evidence.fact: First ascent credited to Fred Beckey and party in 1963.

facts.value: Slesse Memorial trailhead (Nesakwatch Creek FSR)

evidence.fact: Park at the Slesse Memorial trailhead where the road widens; a thin signpost marks the trail.

facts.value: Slesse Memorial trail to the propeller cairn (~3 hrs), then slabs, a 3rd/4th-class gully and notch into the bypass glacier cirque; ~4 hrs to the bypass ledge

evidence.fact: Trail to the propeller cairn about 3 hours; then slabs, a 3rd/4th class gully and notch into the cirque; about 4 hours to the bypass ledge.

facts.value: Icefall from a hidden ledge above the bypass-glacier cirque; cross quickly

evidence.fact: Ice and snow on a ledge above the cirque entrance can fall with little warning; move fast to the middle of the slabs.

facts.value: Pocket glacier: many parties wait until it slides off (July to September depending on year)

evidence.fact: Climbers often wait for the pocket glacier to slide off; some years by July, other years it lingers into September.

facts.value: Glacial ice melt near the bypass ledge; seasonal snow on the mid-height bivy ledge until late July

evidence.fact: Melting glacial ice near the bypass ledge gives water; the bivy ledge snow patch lasts only until late July.

facts.value: Bivy ledge at half height (sleeps up to 6); other bivies at pitches 6, 10, 17, 20, the summit and the descent

evidence.fact: Half-height bivy ledge sleeps up to six; more bivy spots at pitches 6, 10, 17 and 20, the summit and the descent.

facts.value: Most parties take 2 long days: day 1 hike and climb to the mid-height bivy; day 2 finish, descend, hike out

evidence.fact: Most parties take two long days: day one to the half-height bivy, day two summit, descend and walk back to the car.

facts.value: Via Crossover Pass, rappelling the Crack of Noon Club route, back to the Slesse Memorial trailhead

evidence.fact: Preferred descent goes over Crossover Pass and rappels the Crack Of Noon Club route, returning to the Slesse Memorial trailhead.

facts.value: Slesse Creek FSR on the west side is gated and locked by the Canadian military

evidence.fact: The west-side Slesse Creek FSR is now gated and locked by the Canadian military.

facts.value: Logging road condition varies by year; low-clearance cars may not reach the trailhead

evidence.fact: Road condition varies yearly; author reached the trailhead in a Subaru Forester, others could not, especially low-clearance cars.

facts.value: Bypass ledge skips the first 6 pitches of the NE Buttress Direct (5.10c); 5.9 cruxes include pitches 17 and 19; last 7 pitches on the headwall

evidence.fact: The bypass ledge skips the first six pitches of the Direct (5.10c); 5.9 cruxes at pitches 17 and 19; seven headwall pitches finish.

facts.value: Near the top a ledge leads left into 4th-class terrain to the summit ridge

evidence.fact: Near the top, tired parties can escape left on a ledge into 4th class ground reaching the summit ridge.
Summit elevation given as 2,440 m / 8,002 ft.

bc_slesse_mountain_northeast_buttress.note: SummitPost NE Buttress Bypass page answered 403. No page stated a one-way distance or gain for this route.

evidence.fact: Listed as trad/alpine, 500 ft, 6 pitches, Grade III; six pitches from the northern notch to the summit.
Route length listed as 500 ft (152 m).

facts.value: III

evidence.fact: Route listed as Grade III.

facts.value: Jeff Lowe, Rob Kiesel, July 1972 (as the top of the North Rib)

evidence.fact: FA listed as Jeff Lowe and Rob Kiesel, July 1972; likely first climbed as the final pitches of the North Rib.

facts.value: Reach the northern notch via the west-side trail, then 6 pitches to the summit

evidence.fact: A 1974 party reached the northern notch from the west side trail and climbed six pitches to the top.

facts.value: Steep climbing on mostly solid holds; rock quality not the best

evidence.fact: Rock is not the best quality but the climbing is steep with mostly solid holds.

bc_slesse_mountain_north_pillar.note: Only Mountain Project describes the North Pillar as its own route; the North Rib pages below count it as the last 6 pitches of the North Rib. No distance/gain stated.

evidence.fact: Listed as trad/alpine, 2800 ft, 27 pitches, Grade V.
First-ascent report: NCCS V, F8, 27 pitches, no aid.

facts.value: V

evidence.fact: Route listed as Grade V.
First-ascent report rates it NCCS V.
Route length listed as 2800 ft (848 m).

facts.value: Rob Kiesel, Jeff Lowe, July 1972

evidence.fact: FA listed as Rob Kiesel and Jeff Lowe, July 1972.

facts.value: Rob Kiesel and Jeff Lowe, in July

evidence.fact: FA listed as Rob Kiesel and Jeff Lowe, July 1972.
Jeff Lowe reports climbing the rib with Rob Kiesel in July; 13 hours of climbing with a bivouac atop the rib.

facts.value: Climb the vague rib between Heart of Darkness and the North Face couloir to the notch, then 6 more pitches up the NW arete of the summit tower

evidence.fact: Climb the rib between Heart of Darkness and the North Face Couloir to the notch, then six pitches up the summit tower's NW arete.
FA party climbed the rib on the right of the north face, then the northwest corner to the summit.

facts.value: Cross the North Slesse Glacier to the base; crampons and axe needed

evidence.fact: Cross the North Slesse Glacier, which never melts out, so crampons and an axe are always needed to start.

facts.value: North Slesse Glacier icefall; the glacier reportedly slid in 2024

evidence.fact: Glacier crossing to the base has icefall problems and is called dangerous.
Author believes the whole North Slesse Glacier slid in 2024; treat it with caution, less volatile than the pocket glacier.

facts.value: Full rack plus crampons and ice axe for the approach

evidence.fact: Protection: full rack; crampons and ice axe for the approach.

facts.value: Doubles 0.2-1, singles 2-3, set of nuts; one 70 m rope

evidence.fact: Party carried doubles 0.2 to 1, singles 2 to 3, nuts, and a single 70 m rope with no tag line.
Party climbed the North Rib in a single push, 18.5 hours car to car (August 2025).

facts.value: Crossover Pass descent, finishing with the Crack of Doom rappels

evidence.fact: Descent by the Crossover Pass route, ending with the Crack of Doom rappels, tricky to find in the dark.

facts.value: Water in the open talus field on the way to the base, even late summer

evidence.fact: Plenty of water in the open talus on the approach to the North Rib, even late in summer.

facts.value: Second most popular technical route after the NE Buttress; better rock than the NE Buttress, some long runouts; first third is low-angle runout 5.8

evidence.fact: Probably second most popular technical route after NE Buttress; better rock but some long runouts.
Guidebooks describe runout 5.8 slab for the first third; author found it secure low-angle cracks and flakes.

facts.value: Mid-route snow patch; FA party bivouacked at the top of the rib

evidence.fact: 13 hours of climbing broken by a bivouac at the top of the rib.

bc_slesse_mountain_north_rib_kiesel_lowe.note: Car-to-car 18.5 h is one party's single-day time (North Shore Alpinism). No stated approach distance or gain.

facts.value: Will Kovacic and Jeremy Roulette, early June

evidence.fact: Will Kovacic and Jeremy Roulette climbed the new route on the east side of Mt. Parkes in early June.
They climbed a broken buttress in about nine pitches to the summit of Parkes.
Route named Russian Roulette, graded 5.9.

facts.value: Broken buttress on the east side of Mt. Parkes (ca 2,100 m) on Crossover Ridge north of Slesse; continues along the ridge and upper North Rib to Slesse's summit

evidence.fact: Mt. Parkes (ca 2,100 m) sits on Crossover Ridge north of Slesse; party continued along the ridge and upper North Rib to Slesse's top.
Mt. Parkes given as about 2,100 m.
